questions.problem: Given that  $L{t\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t)}=\frac{{s}^{2}-{\omega }^{2}}{({s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2})^{2}},$ find the Laplace transform $L{{e}^{4t}\cdot t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The first shifting theorem states that if
$L{f(t)}=F(s),$
then
$L{{e}^{at}f(t)}=F(s-a).$

Using the given result, we have

$$
L{t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)}=\frac{{s}^{2}-{3}^{2}}{({s}^{2}+{3}^{2})^{2}}.
$$

Therefore, applying the first shifting theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{4t}\cdot t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)} & =\frac{(s-4)^{2}-{3}^{2}}{((s-4)^{2}+{3}^{2})^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(s-4)^{2}-9}{((s-4)^{2}+9)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Applying the First Shifting Theorem and Linearity
questions.problem:
Given that

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{t}^{n}} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}, &  & s>0,\end{aligned}
$$

use linearity of Laplace transforms and the first shifting theorem to find the Laplace transform of  $f(t)=5{e}^{-t}+3{t}^{3}{e}^{2t}$ for $s>2.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we apply the linearity properties of Laplace transforms:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =L{5{e}^{-t}+3{t}^{3}{e}^{2t}} \\  & =L{5{e}^{-t}}+L{3{t}^{3}{e}^{2t}} \\  & =5L{{e}^{-t}}+3L{{t}^{3}{e}^{2t}}\end{aligned}
$$

We are given that, for $s>0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{t}^{n}} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{t}^{3}} & =\frac{6}{{s}^{4}}\end{aligned}
$$

The first shifting theorem states that if $L{f(t)}=F(s),$ then $L{{e}^{at}f(t)}=F(s-a).$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{t}^{3}{e}^{2t}} & =\frac{6}{(s-2)^{4}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =5L{{e}^{-t}}+3L{{t}^{3}{e}^{2t}} \\  & =5\cdot \frac{1}{s+1}+3\cdot \frac{6}{(s-2)^{4}} \\  & =\frac{5}{s+1}+\frac{18}{(s-2)^{4}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This transform is valid for $s>2.$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Graph Shifts From the First Shifting Theorem
questions.problem: Consider a function $f(t)$ for which the Laplace transform is $L{f(t)}=F(s).$ How can we obtain the graph of $L{{e}^{3t}f(t)}$ from the graph of $F(s)?$
questions.worked_solution:
The first shifting theorem states that if
$L{f(t)}=F(s),$
then
$L{{e}^{at}f(t)}=F(s-a).$

This implies that multiplying a function $f(t)$ by ${e}^{at}$ shifts the corresponding Laplace transform horizontally along the $s$-axis.

- If $a>0,$ the graph of $F(s)$ shifts to the right.

- If $a<0,$ the graph of $F(s)$ shifts to the left.

In our case, to get the graph of $L{{e}^{3t}f(t)},$ we must shift the graph of $F(s)$ by $3$ units to the right.

choices.value: Scale the graph of $F(s)$ by a scale factor of $3$ vertically.
Shift the graph of $F(s)$ by $3$ units to the left.
Shift the graph of $F(s)$ by $3$ units to the right.
Scale the graph of $F(s)$ by a scale factor of $3$ horizontally.

answer_fields.correct_value: Shift the graph of $F(s)$ by $3$ units to the right.

questions.problem:
Consider a function $y(t)$ such that its Laplace transform is $L{y(t)}=Y(s)$ for $s>{s}_{0}.$ Suppose we wish to find $L{{e}^{4t}y(t)}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write 

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{4t}y(t)} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-1}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-2}}\,y(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={{field-3}}\,\text{for}\,{{field-4}}.\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{4t}y(t)} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{4t}\,y(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s-4)t}\,y(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that $Y(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,y(t)\,\text{d}t,$ where $s>{s}_{0}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s-4)t}\,y(t)\,\text{d}t=Y(s-4),
$$

where 

$$
s-4>{s}_{0}\,⇒\,s>{s}_{0}+4.
$$

Now, recall that $G(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,g(t)\,\text{d}t,$ where $s>{s}_{0}.$ Therefore,

{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s+3)t}\,g(t)\,\text{d}t=G(s+3),
$$

where 

$$
s+3>{s}_{0}\,⇒\,s>{s}_{0}-3.
$$

provenance.kp_title: Proving the First Shifting Theorem

canonical_examples.problem: Given that $\mathcal{L} \left\{t\sin(\omega t) \right\}=\dfrac{2\omega s}{(s^2+\omega^2)^2},$ find the Laplace transform $\mathcal{L}\left\{e^{-5t}\cdot t\sin(2t)\right\}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The first shifting theorem states that if
$\mathcal{L}\left\{f(t)\right\} = F(s),$
then
$\mathcal{L}\left\{e^{at}f(t)\right\}  = F(s-a).$

Using the given result, we have

$$
\mathcal{L}\left\{t\sin(2t) \right\} = \frac{2(2)s}{(s^{2}+2^2)^{2}}.
$$

Therefore, applying the first shifting theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{-5t}\cdot t\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)} & =\frac{2(2)(s+5)}{((s+5)^{2}+{2}^{2})^{2}} \\  & =\frac{4(s+5)}{((s+5)^{2}+4)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Applying the First Shifting Theorem and Linearity
canonical_examples.problem:
Given that

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{t}^{n}} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}, &  & s>0,\end{aligned}
$$

use linearity of Laplace transforms and the first shifting theorem to find the Laplace transform of  $g(t) = 2t^2 + 5te^{4t}$ for $s > 4.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we apply the linearity properties of Laplace transforms:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{g(t)} & =L{2{t}^{2}+5t{e}^{4t}} \\  & =L{2{t}^{2}}+L{5t{e}^{4t}} \\  & =2L{{t}^{2}}+5L{t{e}^{4t}}\end{aligned}
$$

We are given that, for $s > 0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{t}^{n}} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{t} & =\frac{1}{{s}^{2}} \\ L{{t}^{2}} & =\frac{2}{{s}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

The first shifting theorem states that if $\mathcal{L}\left\{f(t)\right\} = F(s),$ then $\mathcal{L}\left\{e^{at}f(t)\right\}  = F(s-a).$ Therefore,

$$
\mathcal{L}\left\{ te^{4t} \right\} = \dfrac{1}{(s-4)^2}.
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $g(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{g(t)} & =2L{{t}^{2}}+5L{t{e}^{4t}} \\  & =2\cdot \frac{2}{{s}^{3}}+5\cdot \frac{1}{(s-4)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{4}{{s}^{3}}+\frac{5}{(s-4)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This transform is valid for $s>4.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Identifying Graph Shifts From the First Shifting Theorem
canonical_examples.problem: Consider a function $f(t)$ for which the Laplace transform is $\mathcal{L}\{f(t)\} = F(s).$ How can we obtain the graph of $\mathcal{L}\{e^{-6t} f(t)\}$ from the graph of $F(s)?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The first shifting theorem states that if
$\mathcal{L}\left\{f(t)\right\} = F(s),$
then
$\mathcal{L}\left\{e^{at}f(t)\right\}  = F(s-a).$

This implies that multiplying a function $f(t)$ by $e^{at}$ shifts the corresponding Laplace transform horizontally along the $s$-axis.

- If $a > 0,$ the graph of $F(s)$ shifts to the right.

- If $a < 0,$ the graph of $F(s)$ shifts to the left.

In our case, to get the graph of $\mathcal{L}\{e^{-6t} f(t)\},$ we must shift the graph of $F(s)$ by $6$ units to the left.

canonical_examples.problem: Consider a function $f(t)$ such that its Laplace transform is $\mathcal{L}\{f(t)\} = F(s)$ for $s>s_0.$ Suppose we wish to find $\mathcal{L}\{e^{-7t} f(t)\}.$ Show the steps to compute this transform.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{-7t}f(t)} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{-7t}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s+7)t}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that $\displaystyle F(s) = \int_0^{\infty} e^{-st} \, f(t)\, \textrm{d}t,$ where $s > s_0.$ Therefore, 

$$
\int_0^{\infty} e^{-(s+7)t} \, f(t)\, \textrm{d}t = F(s+7),
$$

where 

$$
s + 7 > s_0
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad 
s > s_0 - 7.
$$
